Commendation

/kom-en-DAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Commendation means a formal, official statement or act of praise, such as an award or citation.

Commendation means a formal, official statement or act of praise, such as an award or citation. The museum's trustees voted unanimously to issue a written commendation to the conservator who saved the fire-damaged murals.

Worked Example

When the ransomware attack froze the hospital's systems, night-shift pharmacist Ellis Okafor hand-checked every medication order against paper records for eighteen straight hours, and not one dose went out wrong. Two months later, the hospital board did something it had done only four times in its history: it entered a formal commendation into the official record, praising Okafor by name and describing exactly what his diligence had prevented.

The board's formal, on-the-record statement of praise — voted on, written down, and entered into the official record — is what makes this a commendation rather than a simple thank-you.

How Commendation Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

citation

citation: an official mention honoring someone

tribute

tribute: a public act of honor or respect

Antonyms

condemnation

condemnation: a formal statement of disapproval

criticism

criticism: fault-finding disapproval

How Strong Is It? — compliment → commendation → medal

compliment vs. commendation

compliment vs. commendation: A compliment is casual, everyday praise; a commendation is official praise made formally and on the record.

medal vs. commendation

medal vs. commendation: A medal goes one step past a commendation — the official praise becomes a physical decoration pinned on for all to see.

Sort It Out

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com-

Prefix — com-: with; fully (Latin)

Root — mend

Root — mend: to entrust, to commit (Latin mandare)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Commendation combines the Latin prefix com- ('fully') with mandare, 'to entrust' — to commend someone was originally to entrust them, fully and publicly, to another's good opinion. The same root powers recommend and mandate. The suffix -ation turns the act into a thing: the official document or statement in which that public entrusting of praise is recorded.

Use the root in a new word: mandate

Use the root in a new word: mandate: A mandate is authority formally entrusted to someone — the same Latin root mandare, 'to entrust,' that sits inside commendation.
